item.title: Early-Buyer Groups and Fast-Wallet Teams on a Bonding-Curve Launchpad: A Prospective Measurement Study of pump.fun on Solana
item.description: We study coordinated groups of wallets on a bonding-curve launchpad (pump.fun on Solana), using a complete record of 200\,443 token launches, 15\,854\,121 curve trades and 51\,025\,958 SOL transfers over 88.3 hours. A prospective, multi-channel discovery procedure (co-buying, shared funding, joint signing, transfers, consolidation) yields 23\,710 wallet groups. Without ground-truth labels we validate them by out-of-sample link prediction, independent non-trading links and a comparison with naive co-buy clustering at equal numbers of flagged tokens: raw clustering collapses into one giant component, yet it ranks tokens at least as well as the groups, so the value of the structure is descriptive. Group activity is highly concentrated and splits into serial creators and long-lived rings of early buyers. Known members buy earlier than other buyers of the same token and extract more cash than an activity-matched placebo set, while late buyers' net cash flow is negative; tokens with members show a pump-like price path, but the contrast vanishes when controls are restricted to comparable tokens, so we report it as an association. A follower entering at the earliest group signal loses money out of sample in all 32 configurations and does no better than random entry. A few pools of tens to over a hundred fast wallets are associated with a two- to four-fold higher chance of reaching 20 SOL, also within creators, with a smaller excess at 60 SOL and none for graduation; on a final hold-out the team rules keep a precision of about one half to three quarters, yet many signals arrive when the curve already holds 20 SOL, one team supplies most of them, and they add no information beyond early curve state. We also document evaluation errors that turn the same data into apparent profit.

item.title: Calibration of Passive Market Impact with a Queue-Sensitive Propagator Model
item.description: We develop a framework for calibrating passive market impact, defined as the price response to liquidity-providing limit orders, in contrast to the impact of liquidity-consuming market orders. We build on the model of Ouazzani Chahdi, Rosenbaum, and Szymanski (arxiv:2412.07461), which combines Hawkes-driven market-order flow with queue-reactive limit-order and cancellation dynamics. Within this model, we show that the price decomposes into a universal propagator term driven by signed order-flow imbalance and a state-dependent correction that captures the dependence of price sensitivity on volume at the best quotes. This decomposition links limit-order-book microstructure to standard propagator models and yields a regression on two observable signals: the propagator signal and the queue-weighted order-flow imbalance. We calibrate the model on high-frequency order-book data and find that the passive-impact term explains substantial variation in prices beyond the classical propagator, improving both model fit and the accuracy of predicted impact curves.

item.title: Optimal Order Placement under a State-Dependent Hawkes Process Limit Order Book model
item.description: We study optimal quote placement for a market maker facing order flow modeled by a state-dependent Hawkes process. A block-based linear demand specification links market-order counts to execution volumes, providing the demand moments required by a continuous time discrete state dynamic programming formulation. Under a quadratic terminal inventory penalty, we characterize inventory-dependent quotes and derive backward recursions for the coefficients of a quadratic value function. Numerical experiments using LOBSTER data examine quote distributions, inventory exposure, and terminal wealth. The implemented strategy yields higher aggregate terminal wealth than fixed-spread benchmarks at one and three ticks, but lower wealth than the two-tick benchmark. These results illustrate the framework's numerical implementation and distinguish terminal-wealth comparisons from evaluation under the inventory-penalized objective.

item.title: Depositing More Should Not Earn Less: Supplier Income Monotonicity and Rate Curve Design in Pooled Lending Markets
item.description: In utilization dependent interest rate models, adding liquidity can reduce a supplier's total interest income even as the supplier's balance increases. A supplier holding a fraction $α$ of final pool supply keeps income nondecreasing with a marginal deposit exactly when $α(1+η)\leq1$, where $η$ is the elasticity of the borrow rate with respect to utilization. When the condition fails, the supplier can instead raise its income by withdrawing, which pushes utilization further up. On two public Drift markets, a lender held more of the pool than the curve protected in at least one hour in nine on SOL and one in thirteen on USDC. A protocol turns this into a design constraint by choosing, at each utilization, the largest supplier share it intends to protect. That choice caps the elasticity, and integrating the cap describes every admissible curve. Protecting the same share at every utilization gives a power law boundary, and protecting every fresh depositor gives a hyperbolic one. On a multiple kink USDT market, compliant repairs can lower or raise supplier income, because the constraint governs how income responds to a deposit and not the price level.

item.title: Event definition and the branching ratio: Hawkes estimates of price-change clustering in the consolidated quote feed
item.description: Hawkes models of price changes in the consolidated US quote feed find a sub-millisecond kernel component and a branching ratio near criticality. We show that in large-tick stocks the first is the feed's construction: half of NBBO changes are locks or depleted quotes, resolved within a millisecond, which the model reads as excitation. Defining the event as a mid-price level persisting for one millisecond removes the component. Raw fits put three times the clean kernel mass within one second, which a simulation reproduces. Since the total branching ratio trades off against the baseline, we report kernel mass on a fixed window.

item.title: Decorrelating the Advice Layer: A Calibrated Fragility Metric and Tested Mitigations for Synchronized Liquidation in Agentic Wealth Management
item.description: Conversational AI agents are turning wealth management into a continuous loop of market analysis, allocation, risk checks and execution, run for millions of clients on a handful of foundation models. We build a multi-asset agent-based model of this layer, calibrated to measured model concentration, cross-model correlation, retail turnover and 33 years of real equity returns, and ask when the layer amplifies market declines and what prevents it. The effective number of independent decision-makers is bounded however many clients the layer serves: about 2.0 at today's consumer concentration. This monoculture of views drives crowding in individual securities and sets the blast radius of a compromised model provider, but it does not drive market-wide liquidation. Index tail losses rise with the square root of agentic adoption, are 1.47-1.90 times larger under an agentic than under a periodic robo-advice architecture, and do not rise with model concentration; synchronized automation (risk overlays, drawdown cuts and attention-driven execution) drives them. A fragility index computed from aggregate flow, public returns and an impact estimate forecasts tail liquidation out of sample (hold-out R^2 of 0.56) far better than concentration or correlation measures. Decorrelating the automation, not the models, works: dispersing overlay parameters, staging execution and a participation breaker together cut tail liquidation by 63% at no measurable cost to client welfare, whereas provider diversification has no effect. Because the statistics required are sums, they can be computed across platforms under secure aggregation with differential privacy at negligible cost for realistic client populations. In historical replays, an agentic layer holding 10% of the market would have deepened the 2020 crash by about 858 basis points.

item.title: FinLLM-KG: Knowledge Graph-Enhanced LLMs for Financial Sentiment Analysis in Algorithmic Trading
item.description: Recent advances in Generative AI have substantially improved financial sentiment analysis through post-trained financial large language models (LLMs). However, existing approaches remain confined to predicting the sentiment of each article in isolation and operate as black boxes, which limits contextual understanding and hinders deployment in high-stakes financial decision-making. To this end, we introduce FinLLM-KG, a model-agnostic framework that combines causal LLMs with a financial knowledge graph, in order to inject temporally grounded, company-level knowledge from SEC 10-K filings at inference time, without updating model weights. Within FinLLM-KG, context is supplied either as a natural-language company profile or as a small set of relevance-ranked factual triples. This enables sentiment predictions to account for broader firm-level information rather than the article alone, at almost zero computational cost and for any causal LLM. In addition, attributing each article-level sentiment score to individual sentences and to the retrieved knowledge-graph facts makes the evidence behind the prediction inspectable, thereby enhancing explainability and supporting human-in-the-loop review. Simulations demonstrate that FinLLM-KG consistently improves portfolio performance over the state-of-the-art baseline.

item.title: Fuji: The Shape, Composition, and Spread of Demand Bursts on Robinhood Chain
item.description: Demand on blockchain-based marketplaces arrives in bursts and at a high rate. On these platforms the data are completely visible, which makes it feasible to compare the bursty demand against the usual load. The congestion manifests as an increased demand for gas, the primary resource a blockchain sells. Existing studies consider how to price the gas. The demand itself, and what it is made of during bursts, has not been measured. We measure it on Robinhood Chain, a layer-2 blockchain that quickly became a venue for trading tokenized equities and memecoins. We collected the data from every block of its first three active months and more than 50 million Uniswap swaps that occurred during bursty periods. We find that a burst trades about as many pools as a quiet period, mostly different ones, and trades them harder, on top of elevated demand that accumulated for hours. With the bursts aligned on their peaks, the median peak is 2.5 times the usual load. Both the rise and the fall of the demand are described by the sum of two exponential functions with different timescales, a slow one of hours and a fast one of minutes. Against a matched quiet period, a burst has 1.05 times the pools, 1.40 times the trades, and 1.21 times the senders. We use two models to explain the arrival of bursts: externally triggered cascades and self-excitation. The former fits the data relatively better. Inside a burst, the entry of each trader into a pool is followed for about 24 seconds by more entries than the existing traders predict. Whether this is because of imitation or because of a shared signal is left open.

item.title: Do Round Numbers Hold Prices? Occupation Densities and Depth-Conditioned Hazards in the Limit Order Book
item.description: Prices cluster at round numbers, a pattern often interpreted as evidence that these levels act as price barriers. This pattern also admits a mechanical explanation: more liquidity rests there, and prices take longer to leave deeper queues. Limit order book data allow us to distinguish these mechanisms through a tick-grid framework in which local time counts departures and level-wise volatility reflects the departure hazard. Using data for five Nasdaq stocks throughout 2025, we find that round levels attract more liquidity but do not exhibit longer depth-adjusted durations. Intel and SoFi show directional effects, with departures biased away from round levels.

item.title: Tracking High-Frequency Trading Activity in China and Its Effects on Market Quality
item.description: We develop a new order-level proxy for high-frequency trading (HFT) activity based on precise order placement and study its effects on market quality. With quotes updating multiple times per second, millisecond-level order-book access makes high-frequency traders more likely to submit active exact-match orders, defined as limit orders priced exactly at the prevailing best opposite-side quote. Using Shenzhen Stock Exchange data, we validate the proxy: active exact-match orders respond faster to quote updates, cancel more rapidly, concentrate when depth imbalance is favorable and spreads are narrow, and predict mid-quote returns from 100 milliseconds through ten minutes. A difference-in-differences design exploiting cross-channel variation in order dissemination latency at the market open shows that lower latency increases active exact-match shares. This variation yields plausibly causal evidence that latency-induced HFT raises short-horizon price variation, wide-spread incidence, and adverse-selection exposure, while realized spreads decline and pricing error falls modestly. Unlike developed markets, China's T+1 constraint, absence of maker-taker rebates, and limits on rapid quote revision tilt speed advantages toward directional liquidity taking, highlighting how market design shapes the channel through which speed affects market quality.

item.title: Optimal Size in Market Making under State-Dependent Hawkes Process
item.description: We study market making with a parametric model of executed volume that accounts for quote placement and state-dependent order flow. Executed volume is expressed as the product of an average order size, an exponential demand function, and a Prony-series multiplier depending on quote depth, market-order count constructed from a state-dependent Hawkes model. An approximation result for finite Prony sums on a compact state domain provides a mathematical basis for the representation. An empirical study of limit-order-book data examines the calibrated demand and intensity models, sensitivity to inventory restrictions, and the resulting placement policies. In retrospective evaluations conditional on realised order-flow paths, the selected calibration achieves higher terminal utility than a baseline while respecting the prescribed inventory bound. The comparisons also distinguish the contribution of trading revenues from that of inventory control. The resulting closed-form volume specification takes placement levels as inputs and can therefore be used with alternative quoting rules.
